Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Vulnerability: Being naked, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Vignette:
Bao, a forty-six-year-old software engineer, described his life as having been lived within a fortress of his own making for the better part of two decades. The walls were the familiar rooms of his suburban home, and the perimeter was the front door he rarely passed through. It was from this self-imposed confinement that he finally sought help. The event that had built this fortress was a lifetime away, but for Bao, it was as immediate as the scent of gasoline from his neighbour’s lawnmower. He was a young soldier then, stationed in a humid, remote jungle outpost. His unit had been granted a rare moment of respite by a slow-moving river. The air was thick with the smell of diesel from a sputtering generator and damp, overturned earth. Men were laughing, washing the grime from their bodies and clothes. Bao was among them, standing half-undressed on the riverbank, feeling the acute vulnerability of being exposed and unarmed. It was in that moment of peace that the high-pitched, metallic whine of two-stroke engines tore through the air. The sound was alien, then terrifying. Motorcycles, two of them, burst from the dense foliage, and the world dissolved into the crackle of automatic fire.

That memory does not exist for Bao as a coherent story. When he tries to explain it, he falters, stating that he simply can't seem to put the frightening event into words. Instead, it lives inside him as a sensory loop, a short, brutal film that plays over and over without his consent. The clip is always the same: the smell of diesel, the feeling of utter helplessness while being naked and exposed, and the piercing sound of the engines. This nonverbal replay is so powerful that it bleeds into his present. When a delivery driver’s moped sputters down his quiet street, Bao doesn't just hear the engine; in his head, the sound is immediately followed by the phantom crackle of gunfire he heard during the ambush.

His life has since become a complex architecture of avoidance. As a software engineer who now works primarily from home, he has been able to shrink his world to a manageable size. He avoids going out unless absolutely necessary, his justification to his wife, Mai, being that he cannot assess the danger of unfamiliar places. He cannot map the exits, he’d explain, or know where a threat might come from. A simple invitation to a new restaurant is met with refusal. He has stopped exercising entirely; the thought of being in a locker room, surrounded by strangers while feeling exposed, is intolerable. The consequences have accumulated slowly. He turned down a promotion that would have required travel, and his social circle has dwindled to almost nothing. Mai feels she is living with a ghost, a husband who is physically present but emotionally barricaded. She learned long ago to stop suggesting they watch action movies; the sight of anything resembling combat on screen would cause Bao to leave the room without a word.

Even within his fortress, there is no peace. Bao feels on guard even inside his own home, checking locks and startling at the sound of a car door slamming. He feels threatened by strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations; a mail carrier walking up his driveway can trigger a surge of adrenaline, a cold certainty of imminent danger. Showering has become a hurried, tense ritual performed behind a locked door, the feeling of being naked bringing with it a prickling dread that only subsides once he is fully clothed again. He has come to believe the world outside his home is fundamentally unsafe and that his hypervigilance is the only thing keeping him alive. It was after a particularly severe panic attack, triggered by a group of teenagers riding dirt bikes in a nearby park, that Mai finally insisted he seek help. Bao agreed, not out of hope, but out of a profound exhaustion. He is terrified that he is losing his wife and his life, and what frightens him most is the unshakeable feeling that the film in his head will never, ever stop playing.
